an0091.user: Pet-care brand, Meesho ads. I'd like the sharp read. Over six weeks my CAC climbed from ₹595 to ₹1,166 and ROAS fell from 3.1 to 1.6. AOV ₹1,850, margin 42%. Frequency's at 3.4. Creative and audience are unchanged — same setup that was working. Algorithm problem?
an0091.assistant:
Not the algorithm — and the sharp read is that your thin margin has turned ordinary creative fatigue into an outright loss.

Contribution per order: ₹1,850 × 42% − ₹1,166 = ₹777 − ₹1,166 = −₹389. Six weeks ago at ₹595 CAC you cleared ₹182 an order. Now you lose ₹389. Your 42% margin gives you very little cushion, so when CAC nearly doubled, you blew straight through breakeven.

The cause is sitting in your own numbers: frequency 3.4 and a sliding CTR, against unchanged creative and audience. Above ~2.5, frequency means the same people are seeing the same ad on repeat; at 3.4 they've tuned it out, clicks fall, and Meesho charges more to keep serving an ad people ignore. That's creative fatigue, plainly. The algorithm and targeting are constant — that's the whole reason they can't be the cause. Steady inputs, collapsing output: the variable that moved is audience patience.

Two moves, in order. First, urgent: get genuinely new creative live this week — new angles and hooks, not a recolour — because every day on the tired ad costs ₹389 an order. Second, structural: your 42% margin leaves no room for error, so a CAC that drifts even ₹100 sinks you. Build a testing cadence so a fresh challenger is always queued, and hold CAC under your ₹777 breakeven like your life depends on it — at this margin, it does.

an0092.user: Candle brand, mostly organic traffic. Here's the funnel, last 30 days: 48,000 visits, 3,753 add-to-cart, 2,319 reached checkout, 604 bought. CTR's 1.6%. I'm convinced my traffic quality has dropped and I need better visitors. Right?

Your traffic is fine — let the funnel show you where the money actually leaks, because more visitors would just feed a leak you haven't fixed.

48,000 visits → 3,753 add-to-cart is about 8%. Healthy; people want your candles. Add-to-cart → checkout, 3,753 → 2,319, is 62% — also fine. Now the cliff: 2,319 reached checkout, 604 bought. That's a 26% checkout-to-purchase rate, when a working checkout lands around 50–70%.

So roughly 1,700 people a month walk all the way to the payment step, wallet out, and quit. That's the leak — the very last step, after they've already decided to buy. It has nothing to do with traffic quality; these are your best, most-committed visitors, and the store is losing them at the till.

What kills people at checkout is a short, fixable list: shipping cost revealed late, a forced account-creation wall, no UPI or COD, a mobile payment step that stumbles. Go buy something from your own store on your phone right now and watch where you hesitate. Recover even half of those 1,700 and you've added ~850 orders a month without a single extra visitor. Fix the checkout before you spend a rupee chasing traffic.

You're acquiring brilliantly into a business that forgets its customers, so your lifetime value barely exceeds that single ₹627.

Here's why scaling now is a trap: more spend buys more first orders at a rising CAC as you exhaust your best audiences, and not one of them compounds into repeat revenue. You'd be pouring water into a bucket with no bottom — faster, and more expensively. The great ROAS makes the trap feel like an opportunity.

Fix the bottom first. A home-care buyer needs the product again in weeks — so why aren't they back? Set a reorder reminder timed to run-out, a subscribe-and-save, a 30-day follow-up offer. Move repeat from 6% toward 25% and the same spend suddenly pays you two and three times over. Then — and only then — scale that beautiful acquisition.
